doc.title: Roy Haynes — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Boston drummers, the Hip Ensemble and Ellington
title: Jazz Vespers at St. Peter's: Duke Ellington stands for the anthem
summary: The Hip Ensemble closed with the black national anthem, and Ellington and his doctor were first to stand.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Listen. We played at [Pastor John] Gensel’s. He used to have that Jazz Vespers.

I think it was the anniversary of Billy Strayhorn’s death. The church was packed. Adams was with me then. This was the old church. Not the new one there now, in the complex. Not the new one. It was the old St. Peter’s Church on Lexington. Duke Ellington and his doctor – Dr. Logan was a very tall man. We went into that negro national anthem, as it was called, and the first ones to stand up in the church was Duke Ellington and Dr. Logan. Then the whole entire congregation stood up. That was one of the highlights of the Hip Ensemble for me. My kids were little. I remember them getting Duke Ellington’s autograph. So the idea – he knew right off. I would come out of a drum solo, go into [Haynes sings a rhythm, counts off a phrase, and sings the beginning of the melody], and it would slow it down if you go [Haynes sings further]. We’d get down to the end, and Adams would play one of those crescendos, just screeching. Oh boy.
